newsitem.title: UK: Summary of UK Treasury advisers' views on policy.
newsitem.headline: Summary of UK Treasury advisers' views on policy.

text.p: Following is a summary of the views on monetary policy of the six members of the UK Treasury panel of independent forecasters:
KATE BARKER, CONFEDERATION OF BRITISH INDUSTRY

"During (the period) since 1992, there has still been a tendency towards conflict between the Chancellor (of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke) and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George which has at times called into question the credibility of policy. The concern is that this would be more damaging when the economy moved into an above-trend period in which the inflation threat were more severe. Serious consideration should be given to moving towards greater independence for the Bank of England in the setting of interest rates.

The CBI recommendations for this year's budget therefore include a slight tightening of fiscal policy, with tax reductions of at most one billion stg (and arguably nil, if the PSBR data does not show a clear improvement from the prior year), including some reduction in business taxation, as the personal sector is already in robust short-term health."
She forecasts GDP growth of 3.1 percent in 1997 and a 3.5 percent increase in domestic demand, with RPIX falling to 2.4 percent.
PROFESSOR TIM CONGDON, LOMBARD STREET RESEARCH

"The achievement (of medium-term financial stability) of the early and mid-1990s is in jeopardy. The economy is once again on the threshold of a business cycle which will lead to higher inflation in the late 1990s. The period of stability has come to an end.

The right answer on the monetary front is to raise interest rates and to sell government debt exclusively at the long end (ie. away from the banking system).On the fiscal side, the PSBR should be reduced by tax increases and /or expenditure cuts. The monetary measures are far more important than the fiscal, as fiscal action has probably has little effect on national income except in the short run."
He forecasts GDP growth of 4.2 percenrt in 1997 with domestic demand growing by 4.6 percent. RPIX will hit 2.5 percent in 1996 but edge up to 2.9 percent by 1998, he said.
GAVYN DAVIES, GOLDMAN SACHS

"There is a prima facie case for tightening macro policy now. Ideally this should be done through fiscal policy, but it is not realistic in present political circumstances to expect a tightening greater than 0.4 percent of GDP built into the pre-budget baseline; indeed it is questionable whether even that can be delivered.

Thus, the main burden may well fall on the monetary side. There must be a strong presumption that base rates will need to rise in the next 6-12 months, if not sooner. The eventual extent of the rise depends partly on timing, but is unlikely to be any less than the 150 basis points which successfully stabilised the inflation rate in 1994-95."
Davies forecasts GDP growth of 3.4 percent in 1997 with domestic demand growing at 3.2 percent. RPIX will fall to 2.4 percent in 1997 and edge up to 2.6 percent in 1998.
PROFESSOR PATRICK MINFORD, LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY

"All this talk (of rate rises) is entirely premature. Consumer spending is growing moderately well...the problem remains in manufacturing. The case for cutting interest rates now remains. If in due course the economy returns to rude growth, thoughts can then turn to raising them. But we are months if not years away from that situation.

We should push tax rates as low as possible consistent with "sustainable' public finances: effectively public borrowing steady at about 2.0 percent of national income. That bald arithmetic implies taxes could in principle be cut by 12 billion stg.

Given the uncertainties surround public spending plans (particularly those of a possible Labour government) any such figure is too large. However, it could reasonably underpin a rolling programme of planned tax cuts by this government, committed as it is to these spending plans. A 4.0 billion stg tax cut and a standard rate of 22 pence would be a sensible start to such a programme this year."
Mindford forecasts GDP gowth of 3.1 percent in 1997 with domestic demand growing 2.9 percent. He forecasts RPIX at 2.0 percent in 1997 and 2.2 percent in 1998.
BRIDGET ROSEWELL, BUSINESS STRATEGIES LTD

"We have incorporated into our baseline forecasts an increase in interest rates in the second quarter of 1997 of 0.25 percent (this is based on rates standing at 5.75 pecent) followed by further increases through the rest of the year leaving base rates at just over 7.0 percent by the end of 1997. This outome...is the sort we think appropriate. It seem to us not necessarily to be desirable to try and force inflation down below the current rates that we are forecasting in what is likely to be the fastest growth year in the current cycle and therefore one in which inflation is likely to be accelerating.

We have assumed that the most likely outcome is that there will be tax cuts in this budget of around 2.5 billion stg, although in our view there is little justification for such cuts. This is especially the case in the area of consumer spending where growth is likely to be strong."
She forecasts GDP growth of 3.3 percent in 1997 with domestic demand growing 3.6 percent. RPIX will fall to 2.4 percent in 1997 and edge up to 3.1 percent in 1998, she said.
MARTIN WEALE, NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL RESEARCH
"Our forecast shows a chance of about 45 percent that inflation will be 2.5 percent per year or less by the end of next year, and beyond that the situation is likely to deteriorate.

It would be a pity to put up taxes and then find that they had to be reduced again. But the risk is the other way round. To leave taxes unchanged in the hope that the fiscal position can be corrected in other ways over the medium term can easily turn into an excuse for doing nothing about the budget deficit; this would let debt and interest payments increase, adding to the magnitude of the eventual adjustment. Provided interest rate policy is set with fiscal adjustment in mind, there is no reason why tax increases should lead to a slowdown in economic activity."
He forecasts GDP growth of 3.4 percent in 1997 with domestic demand growing 3.4 percent. RPIX will be 2.7 percent in 1997 and edge up to 3.0 percent in 1998.
